France had the largest army in Western Europe and a defensive line it had spent a decade building.

These four snapshots all come from June 1940. Look at how little time separates them.

a thread 🧵🗺️

1/ Panel one, 7 June. Germany had attacked on 10 May, cut the Allied armies in two through the Ardennes, and forced the British off the continent at Dunkirk by 4 June. The second offensive southward, Fall Rot, had just begun.

2/ Panel two, 16 June. Nine days later the front has folded inward. Paris fell on 14 June — declared an open city and left undefended, so German troops simply walked in and photographed themselves at the Arc de Triomphe.

3/ Panel three, 20 June. Axis shading now covers most of northern and central France. Italy had declared war on 10 June and attacked in the Alps, gaining very little ground against French units that were still holding their positions.

4/ Panel four, 22 June — the armistice. Hitler had it signed at Compiègne, in the same railway carriage where Germany had accepted defeat in 1918. The carriage was then shipped to Berlin. The symbolism was the point.

5/ Elapsed time from the first German attack to the armistice: six weeks. The Maginot Line was never seriously broken from the front — it was gone around, through Belgium and the Ardennes, exactly where planners had judged tanks couldn't go.

6/ France was then split: a German-occupied north and Atlantic coast, and a nominally sovereign southern zone governed from Vichy. Somewhere between 1.5 and 1.9 million French soldiers went into German captivity, many for the next five years.

7/ Four maps, fifteen days between the first and the last. Very few great powers have ever come apart this fast.
